subtopics.title: Types of API Policies in Anypoint Platform
subtopics.meta_description: A complete tour of the major out-of-the-box Anypoint Platform policy categories, what each one does in practice, and when to reach for it in API Manager.
subtopics.summary: Anypoint Platform ships a broad catalog of pluggable policies that cover traffic control, identity, and payload security without touching application code.
subtopics.content_html:
One of the biggest advantages of putting an API behind Anypoint API Manager is that you get a library of production-tested policies you can attach declaratively, instead of hand-rolling rate limiting or authentication logic inside every Mule application. Before applying any of them, it helps to know the full catalog and what problem each category solves.

The Policy Catalog

Policies in Anypoint Platform generally fall into a handful of families: traffic management, identity and access control, payload inspection, and message manipulation. The table below summarizes the most commonly used out-of-the-box policies.

Policy CategoryWhat It DoesTypical Use Case
Rate LimitingCaps the number of requests a client can make within a fixed time window (e.g., 1000 requests/hour).Protecting backend capacity from a single noisy consumer.
ThrottlingSimilar to rate limiting but queues or smooths bursts rather than hard-rejecting every excess call.Preventing sudden traffic spikes from overwhelming a downstream system.
Spike ControlLimits the rate of requests processed per second regardless of client identity.Guarding against traffic surges that could destabilize the Mule runtime itself.
Client ID EnforcementRequires a valid client_id/client_secret pair (or just client_id) issued via API Manager contracts.Tracking and controlling which registered applications can call the API.
OAuth 2.0 Token EnforcementValidates bearer tokens against an external OAuth provider before allowing the request through.Securing APIs consumed by applications that already integrate with an identity provider.
JWT ValidationValidates the signature, expiration, and claims of a JSON Web Token presented in the request.Stateless authentication where the token itself carries verifiable identity claims.
IP Allowlist / DenylistRestricts access based on CIDR-defined source IP ranges.Locking an internal API down to a corporate network or blocking known bad actors.
CORSControls which browser-based origins, methods, and headers are permitted to call the API.APIs consumed directly by single-page applications running in a browser.
Basic AuthenticationValidates a username/password pair against a configured security manager.Simple, low-friction protection for internal or legacy-style integrations.
JSON / XML Threat ProtectionRejects maliciously structured payloads (deep nesting, huge arrays, entity expansion attacks).Guarding parsers against denial-of-service and injection-style payloads.
Header Injection / RemovalAdds, rewrites, or strips specific HTTP headers on the way in or out.Enforcing security headers or stripping internal debug headers before a response leaves the gateway.
Custom PoliciesOrganization-authored policies built with the Policy SDK for requirements the catalog doesn't cover.Company-specific rules, such as validating a proprietary signature header.

Grouping Policies by Purpose

It is useful to think of these less as a flat list and more as three functional groups. Traffic management policies (rate limiting, throttling, spike control) exist to protect the backend from load, not to authenticate anyone. Identity and access policies (client ID enforcement, OAuth 2.0, JWT validation, basic auth, IP allowlisting) decide who is allowed to call the API at all. Payload and message policies (threat protection, CORS, header manipulation) operate on the shape and content of the traffic itself, independent of who sent it.

A typical production API instance layers several of these together — for example, client ID enforcement to identify the caller, rate limiting to protect capacity, and JSON threat protection to reject malformed bodies, all applied to the same instance simultaneously.

Example: A Minimal Rate Limiting Policy Configuration

policyName: rate-limiting
config:
  rateLimits:
    - id: default-tier
      maximumRequests: 1000
      timePeriodInMilliseconds: 3600000
  clusterizable: true

Choosing the Right Policy

When deciding which policy to apply, start by asking what you are actually protecting against. If the concern is backend load, reach for rate limiting or spike control. If the concern is unauthorized access, pick an identity policy that matches how your consumers already authenticate elsewhere in your organization — there is little value in introducing a new OAuth provider if every other API already validates JWTs issued by the same identity platform. If the concern is malformed or hostile payloads, threat protection policies belong on any publicly exposed endpoint that accepts JSON or XML bodies.

  • Anypoint Platform policies are grouped into traffic management, identity/access, and payload/message families.
  • Most production APIs combine several policy types on a single instance rather than relying on just one.
  • Rate limiting and throttling protect backend capacity; they do not authenticate callers.
  • Identity policies (client ID, OAuth 2.0, JWT, basic auth, IP allowlisting) determine who may call the API.
  • Threat protection and header policies operate on the message content itself, regardless of caller identity.
  • Custom policies fill gaps when no built-in policy matches an organization-specific requirement.

subtopics.title: How to Apply a Policy: Step-by-Step
subtopics.meta_description: A clear, step-by-step walkthrough of applying, configuring, and verifying a policy on an API instance in Anypoint API Manager, including policy ordering.
subtopics.summary: Applying a policy in API Manager is a guided, no-code process, but verifying it actually took effect and understanding policy ordering both matter just as much.
subtopics.content_html:
Applying a policy sounds like it should be a single click, and largely it is — but there are a few steps along the way that are easy to skip, and skipping them is usually what causes a policy to appear "applied" while doing nothing at runtime. Here is the full walkthrough.

Step-by-Step Walkthrough

  1. Log into Anypoint Platform. Sign in at anypoint.mulesoft.com with an account that has the API Manager permissions needed for the target business group and environment.
  2. Navigate to API Manager. From the platform launcher, open API Manager. Confirm you are in the correct environment (Sandbox vs Production) using the environment selector, since API instances are environment-scoped.
  3. Select the API instance. Click into the specific API instance you want to govern — this is the version of the API registered against a particular environment, not the API specification itself.
  4. Open the Policies tab. Inside the instance, click the Policies tab to see any policies already applied and their current order.
  5. Click Add Policy (or Apply New Policy). This opens the policy catalog, searchable by name or category.
  6. Choose the policy. Select the policy you need, for example Rate Limiting – SLA Based or IP Allowlist.
  7. Configure its parameters. Every policy exposes a configuration form specific to that policy — time windows and request counts for rate limiting, CIDR blocks for IP allowlisting, allowed origins for CORS, and so on. Fill these in deliberately; default values are rarely correct for production traffic.
  8. Save and apply. Click Apply (or Save). Anypoint Platform propagates the policy to the runtime almost immediately for cloud-hosted gateways; self-hosted runtimes pick up changes on their next poll interval.
  9. Verify the policy is active. Call the API instance directly and inspect the response. Many policies leave observable evidence: a rate limiting policy returns HTTP 429 once the limit is exceeded and includes X-RateLimit-Limit / X-RateLimit-Remaining headers; a CORS policy adds Access-Control-Allow-Origin to responses; an IP denylist returns HTTP 403 for a blocked address. If none of these show up, double-check that autodiscovery is correctly wired in the running application and that you tested against the correct environment's URL.

Policy Ordering and Precedence

When more than one policy is applied to the same API instance, order matters. Policies execute as a chain: each inbound request passes through every policy in sequence before reaching the implementation, and the response passes back through them in reverse. API Manager lets you drag and reorder policies in the Policies tab, and the order you choose has real consequences.

A common mistake is placing a rate limiting policy after an expensive JSON threat protection policy that runs on every request, including ones that will ultimately be rejected for exceeding the rate limit. Placing lightweight, rejection-heavy policies (IP allowlist, client ID enforcement, rate limiting) earlier in the chain avoids doing unnecessary work on requests that are going to be blocked anyway. Security-critical policies such as authentication should generally run before anything that inspects or transforms the payload, so that unauthenticated requests never reach payload-processing logic.

Example: What a Verification Call Looks Like

curl -i https://your-org.api.anypoint.mulesoft.com/orders-api/v1/orders \
  -H "client_id: abcd1234" \
  -H "client_secret: secretvalue"

# Expect, for example:
# HTTP/1.1 429 Too Many Requests
# X-RateLimit-Limit: 1000
# X-RateLimit-Remaining: 0

Applying Policies at Scale

For organizations managing dozens of API instances, applying policies one at a time through the UI does not scale well. Anypoint Platform supports applying policies via the Platform APIs and via Anypoint CLI, which is the more practical approach once policy application becomes part of a repeatable governance process rather than a one-off task.

  • Policies are applied per API instance, which is environment-scoped — Sandbox and Production instances are configured independently.
  • Every policy has a configuration form; leaving defaults unexamined is a common source of misconfigured policies.
  • Applying a policy is not the same as confirming it works — always make a verification call afterward.
  • Policy order matters: lightweight, rejection-prone policies should generally run before expensive or payload-inspecting ones.
  • Authentication and access-control policies should typically execute before payload transformation or threat protection policies.

subtopics.title: IP Allowlist and Denylist Policies
subtopics.meta_description: How CIDR-based IP allowlist and denylist policies work in Anypoint API Manager, their key configuration parameters, and the most common real-world use cases.
subtopics.summary: IP allowlist and denylist policies restrict API access by source address using CIDR ranges, offering a coarse but effective first line of defense.
subtopics.content_html:
Not every access-control decision needs to involve tokens or credentials. Sometimes the simplest and most robust control is: only let requests through if they are coming from a known network. That is precisely what the IP Allowlist and IP Denylist policies do in API Manager.

How CIDR-Based Filtering Works

Both policies work by comparing the source IP address of an inbound request against a list of CIDR (Classless Inter-Domain Routing) ranges you configure. A CIDR range like 10.20.0.0/16 represents every address from 10.20.0.0 to 10.20.255.255, letting you describe an entire corporate subnet with a single entry rather than listing thousands of individual addresses.

The allowlist (whitelist) policy takes the opposite approach from the denylist (blacklist) policy: an allowlist rejects everything except the ranges you explicitly permit, while a denylist permits everything except the ranges you explicitly block. You typically use one or the other on a given instance, not both, since they express opposite default postures.

Configuration Parameters

Both policies share a similar shape: a list of CIDR blocks, and a setting for how the client's real IP address should be determined. That second setting matters more than it looks — if the API sits behind a load balancer or CDN, the raw TCP connection IP will be the load balancer's address, not the original caller's. In that case the policy needs to be configured to read the address from a forwarding header such as X-Forwarded-For instead.

policyName: ip-allowlist
config:
  ipExpression: "#[attributes.headers['x-forwarded-for']]"
  cidrBlocks:
    - "10.20.0.0/16"
    - "192.168.100.0/24"
policyName: ip-denylist
config:
  ipExpression: "#[attributes.remoteAddress]"
  cidrBlocks:
    - "203.0.113.45/32"
    - "198.51.100.0/24"

Common Use Cases

The allowlist policy is the natural fit for internal APIs that should never be reachable from outside the corporate network or a trusted set of partner networks — for example, an internal HR system's API that should only ever be called from the company's VPN egress range. Restricting access this way means that even if a client ID were somehow leaked, the request still could not reach the API from an unauthorized network.

The denylist policy fits a different scenario: a public-facing API that should remain open to the general internet, but where a specific range has been identified as a source of abuse — a known botnet range, a compromised partner network, or an IP that has been repeatedly triggering rate limits and appears to be scraping. Rather than tightening rate limits for everyone, you block the offending range directly.

Limitations to Keep in Mind

IP-based filtering is coarse. It says nothing about who a request actually comes from within an allowed range, and it can be circumvented by anyone routing traffic through an already-trusted network (for example, a compromised machine on the corporate VPN). For that reason, IP allowlisting is best treated as a network-layer complement to identity-based policies like client ID enforcement or OAuth 2.0, not a replacement for them. It is also worth remembering that CIDR ranges for cloud-hosted clients (offices behind dynamic ISP addresses, for instance) can change without notice, so allowlists tied to non-static ranges require ongoing maintenance.

  • IP allowlist and denylist policies filter requests using CIDR-notation address ranges.
  • Allowlist denies by default and only permits configured ranges; denylist permits by default and blocks configured ranges.
  • Behind a load balancer or CDN, configure the policy to read the client IP from a forwarding header, not the raw connection address.
  • Allowlisting suits internal or partner-only APIs; denylisting suits public APIs where specific bad actors need to be blocked.
  • IP filtering is a network-layer control and works best paired with identity-based policies, not as a standalone security measure.

subtopics.title: CORS Policy
subtopics.meta_description: What CORS is, why browser-based API clients need it, and how to configure allowed origins, methods, headers, and credentials in the CORS policy correctly.
subtopics.summary: The CORS policy tells browsers which origins, methods, and headers are permitted to call an API directly from client-side JavaScript.
subtopics.content_html:
If an API is ever going to be called directly from a browser-based application — a React single-page app, an Angular admin console, anything running client-side JavaScript on a different domain than the API itself — CORS is not optional. Without it, the browser will silently block the response before your application code ever sees it.

What CORS Actually Is

Cross-Origin Resource Sharing (CORS) is a browser security mechanism, not a server-side concept. Browsers enforce the same-origin policy by default: JavaScript running on https://app.example.com cannot read a response from https://api.example.com unless the API explicitly says it is allowed to. The API says this by returning specific response headers, and CORS support in API Manager is essentially a policy that generates those headers automatically, including handling the preflight OPTIONS request that browsers send before certain kinds of cross-origin calls.

It is important to understand that CORS is not a security boundary against server-to-server calls, curl, or Postman — those never enforce it. CORS only matters for requests initiated by browser JavaScript.

Key Configuration Parameters

ParameterPurpose
Allowed OriginsWhich origins (scheme + domain + port) may make cross-origin requests. Can be a specific list or a wildcard.
Allowed MethodsWhich HTTP verbs (GET, POST, PUT, DELETE, etc.) are permitted from allowed origins.
Allowed HeadersWhich request headers a browser client is permitted to send, e.g. Content-Type, Authorization.
Exposed HeadersWhich response headers the browser's JavaScript is allowed to read beyond the small default set.
Max AgeHow long (in seconds) the browser may cache a preflight response before sending another OPTIONS check.
Allow CredentialsWhether cookies or Authorization headers can be included in cross-origin requests; cannot be combined with a wildcard origin.

A Realistic Configuration

Consider an internal dashboard hosted at https://dashboard.internal.example.com that calls an Orders API and needs to send an Authorization header and read a custom pagination header back.

policyName: cors
config:
  origins:
    - "https://dashboard.internal.example.com"
  accessControlMaxAge: 3600
  exposeHeaders:
    - "X-Total-Count"
  allowCredentials: true
  publicResource: false
  methods:
    - GET
    - POST
    - PUT
  headers:
    - "Content-Type"
    - "Authorization"

Common Pitfalls

The most frequent mistake is using a wildcard (*) for Allowed Origins on an API that also needs Allow Credentials enabled — browsers explicitly reject that combination, since it would let any site on the internet make authenticated requests on a user's behalf. If credentials are required, origins must be listed explicitly.

Another common issue is forgetting that any custom response header the client-side code needs to read — pagination counts, rate limit headers, request IDs — must be listed under Exposed Headers. Browsers only expose a small default set (like Content-Type) to JavaScript unless told otherwise; the header can be present in the raw HTTP response and still be invisible to fetch() or XMLHttpRequest code if it isn't exposed.

Finally, remember that the CORS policy governs preflight and header behavior, but it does not replace authentication. A CORS-enabled API without a client ID or token enforcement policy is still fully open to any caller that isn't a browser.

  • CORS is enforced by browsers, not servers; it has no effect on server-to-server or command-line calls.
  • Allowed Origins, Methods, and Headers control what a browser will permit a page to send; Exposed Headers controls what JavaScript can read back.
  • Wildcard origins cannot be combined with Allow Credentials — browsers will reject that combination outright.
  • Any custom response header the front end needs must be explicitly listed in Exposed Headers.
  • CORS configuration does not authenticate callers; pair it with an identity policy for actual access control.

subtopics.title: JSON and XML Threat Protection Policies
subtopics.meta_description: How JSON and XML threat protection policies guard parsers against denial-of-service and injection-style attacks, with key configuration limits explained.
subtopics.summary: JSON and XML threat protection policies inspect payload structure before parsing to block deeply nested, oversized, or maliciously crafted documents.
subtopics.content_html:
Parsers are one of the least examined attack surfaces in an API. A well-formed but maliciously structured JSON or XML document can consume enormous amounts of memory or CPU before your application logic ever runs, simply by exploiting how parsers work. The JSON and XML Threat Protection policies exist to reject those payloads at the gateway, before they reach the runtime's parser.

JSON Threat Protection

JSON threat protection inspects the structural shape of an inbound JSON body against configured limits, rejecting anything that exceeds them with an HTTP 400 before the payload is ever deserialized into a Mule message.

ParameterWhat It Guards Against
Maximum object entry countObjects with thousands of keys designed to exhaust memory during parsing.
Maximum array element countEnormous arrays that cause excessive allocation or slow downstream processing.
Maximum string value lengthExtremely long string values used to bloat memory or overflow buffers.
Maximum nesting depthDeeply nested objects/arrays that cause stack exhaustion in recursive parsers.
Maximum key lengthAbnormally long property names used for the same exhaustion effect as long values.
 
policyName: json-threat-protection
config:
  maxObjectEntryCount: 200
  maxArrayElementCount: 1000
  maxStringValueLength: 10000
  maxKeyLength: 128
  maxDocumentDepth: 20

XML Threat Protection

XML brings its own class of attacks, the most notorious being the "billion laughs" entity expansion attack, where a tiny document defines nested entities that reference each other repeatedly, expanding into gigabytes of data once parsed. XML threat protection blocks this and related XML External Entity (XXE) attacks by limiting entity expansion and attribute counts, and by disallowing external entity resolution outright.

ParameterWhat It Guards Against
Maximum entity expansionsBillion-laughs style attacks using nested entity definitions.
External entity / DTD resolutionXXE attacks that read local files or make server-side requests via crafted DOCTYPE declarations.
Maximum attribute count per elementElements with thousands of attributes intended to slow or crash the parser.
Maximum document depthDeeply nested elements causing stack exhaustion, similar to the JSON case.
 
policyName: xml-threat-protection
config:
  expandInternalEntities: false
  expandExternalEntities: false
  resolveExternalEntities: false
  maxAttributeCountPerElement: 20
  maxDocumentDepth: 20

Why Structural Checks Happen Before Parsing

The key design point of both policies is that they inspect the raw payload's structure — not its business content — before a full parse is attempted, using lightweight streaming checks. This ordering matters: a naive defense that tries to parse the document first and validate afterward has already paid the CPU/memory cost the attack was designed to inflict. Threat protection policies are deliberately placed early in the policy chain for exactly this reason, alongside authentication policies, so hostile payloads are rejected as cheaply as possible.

Setting Sensible Limits

Limits should be set based on what legitimate traffic actually looks like, not arbitrary defaults. An API that only ever receives flat, shallow order records does not need a nesting depth of 50; setting it closer to 5–10 both blocks abuse and catches integration bugs (like accidental circular serialization) earlier. Conversely, setting limits too aggressively will start rejecting valid large-but-legitimate payloads, such as bulk upload endpoints, so these policies are often applied per-instance rather than globally.

  • Threat protection policies inspect structure before full parsing, rejecting hostile payloads cheaply.
  • JSON threat protection limits object size, array length, string length, key length, and nesting depth.
  • XML threat protection blocks entity expansion (billion laughs) and external entity resolution (XXE), plus attribute and depth limits.
  • These policies should run early in the policy chain, alongside authentication.
  • Limits should reflect realistic payload shapes for the specific API, not one-size-fits-all defaults.

subtopics.title: Basic Authentication (Simple Security Manager) Policy
subtopics.meta_description: How to configure the Basic Authentication policy backed by a Simple Security Manager, and when it makes more practical sense than using OAuth 2.0 instead.
subtopics.summary: The Basic Authentication policy validates a username and password against a configured Simple Security Manager, offering low-friction protection for simpler integrations.
subtopics.content_html:
Not every API needs the full machinery of OAuth 2.0 token issuance and validation. For internal tools, legacy-style integrations, or quick proof-of-concept work, HTTP Basic Authentication backed by a Simple Security Manager remains a practical, low-friction option in API Manager's policy catalog.

How the Policy Works

The Basic Authentication policy expects the client to send credentials via the standard HTTP Authorization: Basic <base64(username:password)> header. When a request arrives, the gateway decodes the header and checks the username/password pair against a Simple Security Manager — a static, configured list of valid users rather than an external identity provider. If the credentials don't match, the gateway returns HTTP 401 with a WWW-Authenticate: Basic challenge header before the request ever reaches the backend implementation.

Because the entire check happens at the gateway layer, the backend application never has to implement any authentication logic itself — it can simply trust that any request reaching it has already been validated.

Configuring the Policy

The Simple Security Manager configuration lists valid username/password pairs (or references a securely stored properties file rather than embedding plaintext passwords directly in the policy configuration). The policy itself is then applied against that security manager.

# Simple Security Manager users configuration
securityManager:
  users:
    - username: reporting-service
      password: "${secure::reporting.service.password}"
    - username: batch-integration
      password: "${secure::batch.integration.password}"
policyName: basic-authentication
config:
  securityManagerName: internal-users-security-manager
  realm: "Orders API"

Where Credentials Are Validated

Validation happens entirely at the API gateway / policy layer, before the request reaches any Mule flow logic in the implementation. This is an important architectural point: the credentials are never seen by application code, which means rotating a password or adding a new consumer is purely an API Manager configuration change, with no redeployment of the underlying application required.

Basic Auth vs OAuth 2.0

The two solve overlapping but different problems, and the choice usually comes down to who the consumer is and what infrastructure already exists.

  • Use Basic Authentication when the set of consumers is small and known in advance (internal services, a handful of partner integrations), when there is no existing OAuth provider to integrate with, or when you need something running quickly for a non-production or low-risk scenario.
  • Use OAuth 2.0 when consumers are external, numerous, or dynamic; when tokens need to expire and be refreshed without sharing long-lived static credentials; when you need scoped access rather than all-or-nothing access; or when the organization already has an identity provider that other APIs authenticate against, and consistency matters.

Basic Authentication also has a real security tradeoff worth naming: the credentials are static and sent on every request (base64-encoded, not encrypted — TLS is what protects them in transit). There is no built-in expiration or rotation mechanism the way OAuth tokens have, so password rotation is a manual, coordinated process between the API owner and every consumer using that credential.

When It's the Right Call

Basic Authentication is a reasonable, deliberate choice — not just a shortcut — for machine-to-machine integrations behind a firewall, for internal batch jobs calling internal APIs, or as a stopgap while a longer-term OAuth integration is being built out. It becomes a liability mainly when it's left in place for externally facing, high-value APIs where credential leakage has broad consequences.

  • Basic Authentication validates credentials from the standard HTTP Authorization header against a Simple Security Manager.
  • All validation happens at the gateway/policy layer; the backend implementation never handles credentials directly.
  • It suits internal, known, and limited sets of consumers better than large or external ones.
  • OAuth 2.0 is generally preferable for external consumers, scoped access, and token expiration/rotation.
  • Credentials should always be stored using secure property placeholders, never in plaintext configuration.

subtopics.title: Custom Policies with the Policy SDK
subtopics.meta_description: An overview of the Policy SDK for building custom Anypoint policies, its YAML definition plus implementation structure, and when a team should build one.
subtopics.summary: The Policy SDK lets teams package organization-specific enforcement logic as a reusable policy when no built-in policy fits the requirement.
subtopics.content_html:
The out-of-the-box policy catalog covers the vast majority of common needs, but occasionally a requirement is specific enough to an organization — a proprietary signature scheme, a legacy header format, a bespoke rate-limiting rule tied to internal account tiers — that no built-in policy fits. That's the gap the Policy SDK closes: it lets a team build, package, and publish its own policy that behaves exactly like a built-in one inside API Manager.

What a Custom Policy Consists Of

A custom policy has two parts working together: a policy definition written in YAML, which declares the policy's metadata, configurable parameters, and the extension points it hooks into; and an implementation, typically a Mule XML fragment (or a compiled extension for more advanced cases) that actually performs the enforcement logic. Once built, the pair is packaged and published to Exchange, after which it appears in the API Manager policy catalog exactly like any Anypoint-provided policy — searchable, configurable through a generated form, and appliable to any API instance.

High-Level Structure of the Definition YAML

# policy-definition.yaml
id: custom-signature-validation
name: Custom Signature Validation
description: Validates a proprietary HMAC signature header on inbound requests.
category: Security
type: custom
resourceLevelSupported: true
configuration:
  - propertyName: sharedSecretName
    name: Shared Secret Property
    type: string
    optional: false
  - propertyName: headerName
    name: Signature Header Name
    type: string
    defaultValue: "X-Signature"
encryption:
  properties:
    - sharedSecretName

High-Level Structure of the Implementation

The implementation file references the parameters declared above and defines the actual Mule logic executed for every request — typically wrapped so it runs before the request reaches the backend flow, similar to how a built-in policy intercepts traffic.

<mule xmlns="http://www.mulesoft.org/schema/mule/core"
      xmlns:http-policy="http://www.mulesoft.org/schema/mule/http-policy">

  <http-policy:proxy name="custom-signature-validation">
    <http-policy:source>
      <choice>
        <when expression="#[not (attributes.headers['{{headerName}}']? default false)]">
          <raise-error type="HTTP:UNAUTHORIZED" description="Missing signature header"/>
        </when>
        <otherwise>
          <http-policy:execute-next/>
        </otherwise>
      </choice>
    </http-policy:source>
  </http-policy:proxy>

</mule>

Building and Publishing

Custom policies are typically developed using the Policy SDK's Maven archetype, tested locally, and then packaged and deployed to Exchange within the organization's business group using the Anypoint CLI or the associated Maven plugin. Once published, the policy becomes available (scoped to that organization, not the whole platform) in API Manager just like any other policy, complete with an auto-generated configuration form driven by the YAML's configuration section.

When a Team Should Build One

Building a custom policy is worth the investment when a rule needs to be enforced consistently across many APIs and many teams — if it's a one-off need for a single API, it is often simpler to implement the logic directly inside that API's flows rather than build, test, version, and maintain a reusable policy artifact. Good candidates include organization-wide header/signature validation schemes, custom rate-limiting logic tied to internal business rules that don't map to the standard SLA-tier model, or translating a legacy authentication scheme that the built-in policies don't natively support.

Before building one, it's worth checking whether combining two or three existing policies (say, header injection plus IP allowlisting) already achieves the same outcome — custom policies add a maintenance burden (versioning, testing, backward compatibility) that a combination of standard policies avoids entirely.

  • Custom policies consist of a YAML policy definition and a separate implementation, packaged together and published to Exchange.
  • Once published, a custom policy appears in the API Manager catalog and configures like any built-in policy.
  • The definition YAML declares configurable parameters that drive an auto-generated configuration form.
  • Custom policies are best built for requirements shared across many APIs, not one-off needs.
  • Check whether existing policies can be combined to meet the requirement before investing in a custom one.
